messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 71 years old, Gus had always taken pride in his work as a security guard. He had spent decades keeping people safe, and it was a job he took very seriously. But that all changed on the day of the terrorist attack at the mall where he worked. Gus was one of the first responders to the scene, and what he saw would stay with him forever. As he recounted the events of that day, Gus's memories were vivid and clear. He remembered the sound of gunfire, the screams of the people running for cover, and the smell of smoke filling the air. But when he talked about it, his voice was flat and emotionless, as if he was describing something that had happened to someone else. Sometimes, he couldn't even put the events into a coherent story – it was all just fragments of chaos. In the months following the attack, Gus began to notice changes in himself. He became hypervigilant, always on the lookout for potential dangers lurking around every corner. When he sat down, whether at home or at work, he insisted on having his back against a wall so he could see the entire room. His family and friends found it peculiar, but to Gus, it was just common sense. Gus also started ruminating about how to get even with the assailants. He spent hours replaying the events in his head, thinking of all the things he could have done differently, and imagining scenarios where he took down the terrorists single-handedly. It wasn't just a matter of revenge – it was about regaining control over a situation that had left him feeling powerless. As time went on, Gus's behavior began to affect his relationships with those around him. His wife, worried about his increasing paranoia, tried to reassure him that they were safe now. But Gus couldn't shake off the feeling that he had failed in his most important role as a protector – not just of others, but also of himself. He felt like he couldn't deal with even the slightest upset anymore, and the thought sent him spiraling into despair. At work, Gus's colleagues noticed that he was becoming increasingly withdrawn. He would sit at his post for hours without speaking to anyone, his eyes scanning the crowds with an intensity that made them uncomfortable. His managers tried to talk to him about it, but Gus just shrugged it off – what did they know? They hadn't been there that day. It wasn't until Gus's wife sat him down and told him she was worried about losing the man she loved that he realized things had gone too far. The thought of his family giving up on him because of his own fears and doubts was a wake-up call – maybe it was time to get some help. As he sat in the therapist's office, Gus couldn't shake off the feeling that he was weak for seeking help, but he knew he needed to try something. He just hoped it wasn't too late to regain control over his life. Gus glanced around the room, his eyes instinctively searching for an exit route and potential threats – old habits die hard. But as he began to talk about what had brought him there, a glimmer of hope flickered in his eyes – maybe this was the first step towards reclaiming his sense of purpose and self-worth.
